findings.fix_hint: move mkstemp inside the try (initialize fd/tmp_path to None) so the OSError handler covers it
findings.problem: `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, ...)` runs before the `try:` block. If the config volume is read-only, full (ENOSPC) or not writable (EACCES), the OSError skips the handler that is meant to swallow it. It escapes through `run_in_executor` into `reset_request_post`, which raises after the token has already been minted and logged. The docstring and the D-17 comments say a file-write failure must not be fatal, but the operator gets a 500 instead of the neutral confirmation.
findings.title: mkstemp sits outside the try, so a failed temp-file create returns a 500 and breaks the non-fatal promise
findings.why_it_matters: On a read-only or full config volume, which is a real NAS setup, the recovery endpoint shows an error page even though a token was minted. The operator may think recovery failed.

findings.fix_hint: track whether fdopen took ownership and os.close(fd) in the except/finally when it did not
findings.problem: The raw fd from mkstemp is only handed to a closing context manager at `os.fdopen`. If `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)` raises OSError (EPERM is common on CIFS/SMB or some NFS mounts), control goes to the except branch. That branch unlinks tmp_path but never calls `os.close(fd)`, and the finally only closes dir_fd. The whole scope is in view and no close happens on this path.
findings.title: File descriptor leaks when os.fchmod fails before os.fdopen takes ownership
findings.why_it_matters: On a filesystem that rejects fchmod, each reset request leaks one fd in the long-running daemon. The 60s rate limit slows this down but does not stop it.

findings.fix_hint: guard last_reset_time/reset_token with a dedicated reset lock, not search_lock
findings.problem: `reset_request_post` takes `app.state.search_lock`. `make_search_job` (scheduler.py:131-226) holds that lock for an entire search cycle, including all Radarr/Sonarr HTTP calls. While a cycle runs, the reset request hangs until it finishes and can hit client or proxy timeouts. Requests that pass the optimistic pre-lock check also pile up on the lock. The lock is only needed to guard the rate-limit and reset_token state, which the search cycle never touches.
findings.title: Unauthenticated reset request waits on search_lock, which search cycles hold for their whole network run
findings.why_it_matters: A locked-out operator may see the reset request hang or time out whenever a slow search cycle is running.

findings.fix_hint: default to float('-inf') or skip the check when the key is absent
findings.problem: With no prior entry, `last` defaults to 0.0, so the check is `time.monotonic() < 60`. On Linux, monotonic usually counts from host boot, so the first request is wrongly rate-limited only within 60s of the host booting. pending: confirm the monotonic epoch on the deployment platform. This mirrors the existing search_now pattern.
findings.title: Rate-limit default of 0.0 can block the first request when time.monotonic() is under 60s
findings.why_it_matters: This is an edge case: a spurious 429 right after the host boots.

logger.warning(
    "Password reset token minted. Read from 'docker logs' or reset-token.txt: {token}",
    token=token,
)
findings.fix_hint: Either route this log line through a sink that is excluded from log_buffer capture (e.g. add a `extra`/filter flag the buffer_sink checks and skips), or add the reset token to a redaction list applied to buffer_sink specifically (even though it's intentionally excluded from the stderr redacting sink), so the token cannot reach `log_buffer`/the web log viewer while still appearing in `docker logs`.
findings.problem: The new code mints a CSPRNG reset token and logs it in plaintext via `logger.warning("...: {token}", token=token)` (routes.py:1689-1692), with an explicit comment asserting 'The token MUST NOT appear in any HTTP response' and that this is 'the ONLY log line that will ever contain the token value', deliberately excluded from `collect_secrets`/the redacting sink (triggarr/logging.py's `create_redacting_sink`). That assumption is false: `setup_logging()` (triggarr/logging.py) also registers a second sink, `buffer_sink`, which captures every log record at or above the configured level (default `log_level='info'`, models/config.py:125, so WARNING passes) into the process-wide `log_buffer` (triggarr/log_buffer.py) WITHOUT any redaction filter applied (the redaction list only contains `collect_secrets()` output, which excludes the reset token by design). `log_buffer.get_recent(30)` is then rendered directly into HTTP responses by two existing, unmodified routes: `GET /` (dashboard, routes.py:382) and `GET /partials/log-viewer` (routes.py:1083), via `triggarr/templates/partials/log_viewer.html` which prints `{{ entry.message }}` verbatim (HTML-escaped, but the secret value itself is fully present in the page text). Both routes require authentication (middleware.py's EXEMPT_PREFIXES do not cover `/` or `/partials/log-viewer`), so this is not reachable pre-auth, but it means ANY authenticated web session — a strictly lower, different trust boundary than the 'operator-only' channels the code intends (docker host/SSH access to read `docker logs`, or filesystem access to read the 0600 `reset-token.txt`) — can read the live reset token for up to 15 minutes (its TTL) or until it rolls out of the 200-entry ring buffer, simply by loading the dashboard or polling the htmx log-viewer partial (which auto-refreshes every 5s). An attacker who obtains any authenticated session (stolen cookie, XSS elsewhere in the app, shared/logged-in browser) can thereby read the reset token and use it (once /reset/confirm is wired up) to set a new password, creating a persistence mechanism that survives revocation of the original session — something the 'operator-only sinks' design was specifically trying to prevent.
findings.title: Reset token leaks into HTTP-rendered log viewer, contradicting the code's own "never in an HTTP response" invariant
findings.why_it_matters: The whole security rationale for logging the token (vs. e.g. emailing it) is that 'docker logs' and the config-volume file require host-level access distinct from the web application's own session/auth boundary. Because the existing in-memory log buffer captures the same message and an unmodified dashboard route renders it, that boundary is silently collapsed: a compromised or borrowed web session becomes sufficient to self-service a password reset, regardless of host access controls.
